title: Planetary-System Architecture as an Additional Constraint on the Drake Equation
content: The Drake equation remains a useful framework for decomposing the problem of extraterrestrial technological civilizations into astronomical, biological and technological factors. Since its formulation in 1961, exoplanet surveys have transformed the empirical basis of the astronomical terms, demonstrating both the ubiquity of planets and a diversity of planetary-system architectures that was unknown when the equation was introduced. Early exoplanet discoveries were strongly biased toward massive short-period planets, particularly hot Jupiters, whereas bias-corrected surveys have shown that hot Jupiters are intrinsically rare and that small planets and compact super-Earth/mini-Neptune systems are common. This paper argues that the conventional term ne can usefully be decomposed into the occurrence of terrestrial planets in nominal habitable zones, nHZ, and an additional planetary-architecture factor farch. The latter is defined as the conditional probability that a nominally habitable terrestrial planet occurs in a planetary-system architecture and evolutionary history compatible with long-term dynamical and environmental habitability. Published dynamical studies are used to motivate provisional sensitivity cases farch = 0.9, 0.5 and 0.1. These are not measured occurrence rates but illustrative permissive, intermediate and restrictive scenarios. The resulting modification scales the classical Drake estimate linearly, so that farch = 0.5 halves the inferred number of contemporaneously detectable civilizations and farch = 0.1 reduces it by a factor of ten. The proposed formulation creates an explicit interface between SETI, exoplanet demographics, planetary formation and celestial mechanics, and identifies a factor that future surveys may progressively constrain.
